paras: The attempted lynching of John D. Tross took place on the West Side of New York City on the evening of April 15, 1903, when a crowd of two to three hundred men and boys chased Tross, a Black man, into a grocery store and fought the police to take him. Police had charged Tross with shooting and seriously wounding Otto Richter, a picture frame maker. Officers held the store until reserves dispersed the crowd, and wire reports carried the episode across the country as a lynching that police had prevented.

Tross, 23, lived at 310 West 39th Street, and Richter lived on the same block, at No. 340. About 7 o'clock Tross left a saloon at Eighth Avenue and 39th Street, where, he said, he had been trying to get work for a friend. He told the police that men insulted him as he left; according to the Evening World, several men followed him to the sidewalk and jeered at him.

Tross then drew a revolver and fired four shots, at Richter according to the police charge, or at the crowd that had gathered according to the Evening World. One bullet struck Richter in the left breast above the heart, though he later said he had been merely an onlooker. The shots drew a crowd that pursued Tross, still holding the revolver, up Eighth Avenue to Daniel J. Quinlan's wholesale grocery at 40th Street. The Evening World wrote that the wounded Richter ran at the head of 300 men and boys, "all shouting for the negro."

Inside the store, the Tribune reported, Tross pushed the pistol into a bag of lima beans before Patrolman McIver, who was off duty, threw him to the floor. Forty or fifty men forced their way in, and two more policemen, named by the Evening World as Flynn and Martin, joined McIver in a struggle that overturned boxes and barrels and nearly wrecked the store. According to the Evening World, Richter and his companions tried to take Tross away from the officers. After the front door was forced shut the crowd tried the 40th Street entrance, and a riot call brought reserves from the West 47th Street station, who kept it out of the store.

Once the crowd dispersed, Tross, who had been "pleading to be saved from what he believed to be an imminent lynching," was taken to the station and locked up. Richter collapsed while describing the shooting at the station and was taken to Roosevelt Hospital, where doctors said the next day that he had a small chance to live. No report was found of Richter's death or recovery, of Tross's arraignment or trial, or of any arrest of members of the crowd.

Two New York papers reported the episode on April 16 in different terms. The New-York Tribune headed it "Riot on the West Side. Negro Charged with Wounding White Man," attributing the shooting to the police charge and giving Tross's account of being insulted. The Evening World built its story around Richter, under "Badly Wounded, He Led Pursuit," while also stating plainly that the crowd had tried "to mob" Tross and fought the police who rescued him.

An Associated Press version, nearly identical to the Tribune's text, ran the same day in the Butte Inter Mountain as "Would Lynch Negro," in the Deseret Evening News as "Shot in a Riot," and on the front page of the San Antonio Daily Light as "Negro Shootist in New York." The San Antonio headline said one shot took "Fatal Effect," although the dispatch beneath it said only that the man was seriously wounded. The Morris Tribune printed the wire on April 18 as "Mob After a Negro. New York Police Prevent Threatened Lynching." No coverage in the Black press was found.

Accounts differ on whom Tross aimed at: the police charged that he fired at Richter, while the Evening World said he fired at the jeering crowd, a version consistent with Richter's own statement that he was only an onlooker. Only the Evening World said that Richter led the crowd and tried to take Tross from the police; the Tribune placed him among the pursuers without describing such an attempt.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John D. Tross
bases: A crowd of hundreds pursued Tross after a shooting, besieged the store where he was seized and fought police to take him, which the wire called a threatened lynching (A1, A2, A9).
A crowd of 200-300 tried to seize Tross from police in retaliation for the shooting of Richter (A1, A2), but he was taken to the station alive (A1), so this was an attempted, not completed, lynching.

Two independent local reports, the Evening World and the New-York Tribune, agree on the shooting, the pursuit, the fight in Quinlan's store and the police rescue (A1, A2); the wire copies derive from the Tribune text (A9).

accounts.gist: Tross drew a revolver and fired four shots at Richter after leaving the saloon; one bullet struck Richter.

accounts.label: Tross's statement
accounts.gist: He had been trying to get work for a friend in the saloon and was insulted by men as he left; he pleaded to be saved from lynching.

accounts.label: Richter's statement
accounts.gist: He was merely an onlooker when shot, and at the station insisted he was not seriously wounded before collapsing.

accounts.label: Evening World reporter
accounts.gist: Men jeered Tross onto the sidewalk and he fired at the crowd; Richter, wounded, led 300 men after him and fought the police to take him.

framing.detail: The Tribune's 'Riot on the West Side. Negro Charged with Wounding White Man' gives the police charge as a charge and reports Tross's account of being insulted.
The Evening World's 'Badly Wounded, He Led Pursuit' makes Richter the protagonist who 'Runs Down the Man Who Shot Him,' while also reporting the attempt to 'mob' Tross and his plea against lynching.

AP copies were headed 'Would Lynch Negro' (Butte), 'Mob After a Negro. New York Police Prevent Threatened Lynching' (Morris), 'Shot in a Riot' (Deseret) and 'Negro Shootist in New York' (San Antonio), the last claiming a shot 'With Fatal Effect'.
